items.title: Kerala HC orders clearance of trash along highway till Kalamassery; will inspect Brahmapuram waste plant
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Friday ordered clearance of waste from identified dumping hotspot in Kochi [Suo Motu v State of Kerala] A Division Bench of Justice Bechu Kurian Thomas and Justice P Gopinath directed the State government to instruct panchayats and municipalities, through which the National Highway 966 passes till Kalamassery municipality, to clear accumulated waste from either side of the road. Pertinently, the Court said that it will be visiting the Brahmapuram waste treatment facility for a physical inspection on September 11 to verify whether it is functioning effectively. The Court said the waste dumped on roads belongs to the government or civil authorities and emphasised their duty to keep public places clean. The Court passed the order in a suo motu case initiated by the High Court to address the issue of waste management in the city. Justice P Gopinath and Justice Bechu Kurian Thomas Justice Thomas expressed concern over continued dumping of waste at various locations in Kochi. " Every two kilometres, there is a huge pile of waste. You can’t expect the court, or the amicus curiae, to point out every time there is a waste accumulated over here, " Justice Thomas told counsel representing Kochi Corporation. The Court then directed the corporation to immediately remove the accumulated waste from locations including the Alexander Parambithara Road towards Cochin Port and Willingdon Island. " Prima facie we are of the view that the moment the waste is dumped on the road, it belongs to the government or to the local authority. Maybe local authorities. Then it is your responsibility to remove irrespective who dumps it and so it is also your responsibility to ensure that waste is not dumped on the road, " Justice Thomas said. The Court also asked the corporation to take effective steps to prevent further dumping and initiate action against those responsible. The corporation was further directed to ensure that the streetscape at Panampilly Nagar is maintained by removing the waste accumulated there. The Bench stressed on the need to change public attitude towards waste disposal and suggested that civic awareness should be imparted through schools. items.title: After barring, backtracking and an inquiry u-turn, BCI chief apologises to NALSAR students
items.summary: The Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman and BJP leader Manan Kumar Mishra has expressed regret and apologised to law students of NALSAR University of Law, without addressing them specifically. In a statement issued on August 15, Manan Mishra addressed law students as ‘My dear young friends’ and said, “If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same.” “There should be no hesitation in saying so. An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter,” he added. The change in tone came about after alumni and students of NALSAR and National Law School of India University (NLSIU), Bengaluru, wrote a letter to the BCI condemning Manan Mishra for his statements and criticising him for clamping down on free speech. On Thursday, August 13, the BCI had asked state bar councils not to enrol students of the 2026 graduating batch of Hyderabad’s National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR) as advocates all because the students had opposed Chief Justice of India’s presence during the annual convocation held in Hyderabad. NALSAR alumni condemn BCI action against students, call it ‘arbitrary’ and ‘coercive’ The directive was rescinded within hours, though the BCI said it would conduct an inquiry based on a report from the university’s Vice-Chancellor before deciding whether any action was warranted against students. A third message then clarified that an enquiry would not take place either. Without directly referring to the NALSAR controversy in his Independence Day message, Mishra stressed that law students, particularly those at National Law Universities, were informed and discerning young citizens capable of forming independent opinions. “They do not require anyone to decide for them,” he said, adding that students should not be subjected to pressure or influence from any quarter. This after he had in his second communication dubbed students as ‘innocent’ and as a group that were ‘instigated’. The BCI chief did not address the NLSUI students’ demand asking that he and the CJI not attend the convocation at NALSAR. Regarding the convocation ceremony, Mishra said: “The decision whether to participate must, of course, ultimately remain with the students themselves. No student should be compelled to attend, and no student should feel compelled to abstain,”

items.title: Delimitation: பாஜகவுக்கு எப்படி பலன் கொடுக்கும்? | CM Vijay | BJP | Shabbir Ahmed | TNM Tamil
items.summary: The debate over delimitation is not only about how many seats a state gains or loses, but also about federalism, political representation and whether population should be the sole basis for determining electoral strength. The 2023 delimitation of Assam has added another dimension to these concerns. Critics have alleged that the exercise diluted the electoral influence of minority voters by concentrating them in fewer constituencies. So, what could a similar exercise mean for Tamil Nadu and other southern states? Is the concern simply about losing constituencies, or is there a larger question about how India’s demographic balance could change? In this week's episode of Yen Endra Kelvi, Shabbir Ahmed examines the politics behind delimitation, the concerns of southern states and what the Assam precedent signals the future of electoral representation in India.
